lessons.title: Ethical and Legal Issues in Digital Technology
lessons.description: Privacy, hacking, cloud storage, wearable tech and the UK laws that protect users and creators.
lessons.content_html:
Why Technology Raises Ethical Questions

Digital technology has transformed how we communicate, shop, access healthcare and use public services. But with those benefits come serious questions: who controls your personal data, what happens when someone accesses a computer without permission, and who owns the software or music you stream? Ethical issues are questions about right and wrong that often have no single correct answer. Legal issues are those that the law defines as permitted or prohibited.

Privacy and Personal Data

Privacy is one of the central ethical concerns of the digital age. Every time you use a smartphone, search engine, social media platform or banking app, data about you is collected. This data may include your location, browsing history, financial transactions, health metrics and social connections. Most people value the ability to control what others know about them, and many feel uncomfortable when they discover how much data organisations hold.

New technologies intensify this challenge:

  • Mobile technologies — smartphones carry GPS sensors, cameras and microphones that can record location and activity continuously. Apps often request permissions to access these sensors beyond what is strictly necessary for the app to function.
  • Wireless networking — public Wi-Fi hotspots can be monitored; poorly secured home routers can expose household devices. Data transmitted without encryption can be intercepted.
  • Cloud storage — saving files to a cloud service means a third-party company holds copies of your data on remote servers. Questions arise about who can access those files and what the provider does with your metadata.
  • Wearable technologies — fitness trackers, smartwatches and medical monitoring devices collect continuous biometric data such as heart rate, sleep patterns and physical activity. This data is highly personal and could affect insurance premiums or employment decisions if shared inappropriately.
  • Computer-based implants — devices implanted in the body (such as pacemakers or neural interfaces) raise profound ethical questions about bodily autonomy, data security and the consequences of a security breach on a person’s health.
Key Fact

Technologies explicitly named in this topic include: mobile technologies, wireless networking, cloud storage, wearable technologies, computer-based implants and autonomous vehicles. For each, you should be able to describe at least one ethical or privacy concern and one benefit.

Hacking and Unauthorised Access

Hacking is the act of gaining access to a computer system without permission. This may involve exploiting security vulnerabilities, using stolen passwords or writing malicious software. Hacking can result in theft of personal data, financial fraud, disruption of services (such as hospital systems going offline) and reputational damage to organisations. Ethically, even “white hat” security researchers who probe systems to find weaknesses must operate within defined legal agreements — probing a system without permission is illegal regardless of intent.

Government Access vs. Citizen Privacy

One of the most debated ethical dilemmas is whether governments and security services should be able to access citizens’ private data. Most people value their privacy and are uncomfortable with the idea of their messages being read or their locations tracked by the state. However, governments and security agencies argue that access to private communications is sometimes necessary to prevent terrorism, serious crime and national security threats. There is genuine tension here, with no universally agreed answer: stronger government surveillance may prevent attacks but also risks misuse of that power and chilling effects on free speech.

Arguments for greater government access: Security services may need to monitor communications to identify terrorist plots before they occur. Without access to encrypted messages, criminals can organise undetected. Proponents argue that citizens with nothing to hide have nothing to fear.

Arguments against: Mass surveillance undermines the presumption of innocence. Governments could misuse data to target political opponents or journalists. Mandatory encryption backdoors would weaken security for everyone, including ordinary users and businesses, since the same backdoor that governments use could also be exploited by criminal hackers.

UK Legal Frameworks

Three key Acts of Parliament govern the legal use of technology in the UK. These are not optional guidelines — breaking them can result in fines, civil claims or criminal prosecution.

The Data Protection Act 2018 governs how organisations handle personal data. It incorporates the requirements of the UK General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR). Organisations must collect data only for a specific, stated purpose; keep it secure; not hold it longer than necessary; and give individuals the right to see, correct or request deletion of their own data. Failure to comply can result in significant fines issued by the Information Commissioner’s Office. This Act replaced the earlier Data Protection Act 1998.

The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes it a criminal offence to access a computer system without authorisation. It covers three categories of offence: unauthorised access to computer material (for example, logging into someone else’s account); unauthorised access with intent to commit or facilitate further offences (for example, accessing a bank’s server to commit fraud); and unauthorised modification of computer material (for example, installing malware or deleting data). A 2015 amendment to the Act increased maximum penalties and added offences relating to attacks on computer infrastructure.

The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 protects intellectual property. Software, music, images, films and written work are automatically protected from the moment of creation. Copying, distributing or publicly performing copyrighted material without permission — whether commercial or personal — is illegal. This is why downloading music or films through unauthorised channels is not just unethical but against the law.

Key Fact

Three UK laws you must know: Data Protection Act 2018 — controls personal data handling; Computer Misuse Act 1990 — makes hacking and malware creation criminal offences; Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 — protects software, music and other creative works from unauthorised copying.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 4-mark or 8-mark questions on ethical or legal issues, examiners reward balance and specificity. If asked to “discuss” or “evaluate”, give arguments on both sides — do not just list benefits. When naming a law, include the year (Data Protection Act 2018, not ‘the 1998 one’) and say what it does, not just its name. Avoid inventing specific clause numbers or case names — a clear descriptive explanation of what each law prohibits earns full marks without invented detail.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Mobile technologies, cloud storage, wearable devices and computer-based implants all raise privacy concerns because they collect personal data that could be accessed or misused by others, including by governments and security services.
  • The Data Protection Act 2018 controls how organisations use personal data; the Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes hacking and malware creation illegal; the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 protects creative works including software.
  • Government surveillance vs. individual privacy is a genuine ethical dilemma with valid arguments on both sides — your exam may ask you to present and evaluate both perspectives.

practice_questions.text: State the name and year of the UK law that makes unauthorised access to a computer system a criminal offence.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering/Secure: Computer Misuse Act 1990. Developing: Computer Misuse Act (no year). Emerging: Any other act named.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why wearable technologies raise ethical concerns about privacy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Wearable devices collect continuous biometric data (heart rate, location, sleep) (1); this data is highly personal and could be shared without the user's knowledge with insurance companies, employers or advertisers (1); users may not fully understand what data is being collected or how to stop it (1); a security breach could expose sensitive health information affecting real-world decisions about a person's life (1). Secure: Two clear concerns with explanation. Developing: One clear concern explained, second is vague. Emerging: Mentions privacy concern without explaining it.

practice_questions.text: Describe what the Data Protection Act 2018 requires organisations to do when handling personal data. Give two requirements.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Organisations must collect data only for a specific, stated purpose and not use it for other purposes (1); they must keep the data secure against loss or unauthorised access (1); they must not hold data for longer than is necessary (1); they must give individuals the right to see, correct or request deletion of their own data (1). Award any two requirements fully explained (2 marks each). Secure: Two requirements stated clearly. Developing: One requirement stated, second vague. Emerging: Act mentioned, no specific requirements.

practice_questions.text: A company collects health data from users' fitness trackers and sells it to insurance companies without telling users. Identify one law the company may be breaking and explain why.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The Data Protection Act 2018 (1); the Act requires that data is collected only for a specific, stated purpose (1); selling health data to insurance companies without informing users goes beyond the stated purpose for which the data was collected (1); this is a breach of the Act which could result in a fine from the Information Commissioner's Office (1). Secure: Correct law named with clear explanation of the breach. Developing: Correct law named but explanation of why it applies is weak. Emerging: Law named with no explanation.

practice_questions.text: 'Governments should be allowed to read citizens' private messages to prevent terrorism.' Evaluate this statement, considering arguments both for and against.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Arguments for — security services may identify threats before they happen; preventing terrorism protects public safety; those with nothing to hide have nothing to fear; legal oversight can limit misuse (2 points, developed). Arguments against — mass surveillance undermines civil liberties; presumption of innocence is eroded; backdoors weaken encryption for everyone; power could be misused against journalists or political opponents (2 points, developed). Conclusion — weighs both sides and reaches a justified personal position (2 marks). Secure: Both sides discussed, some development, weak conclusion. Developing: One side discussed in depth; other side mentioned without development. Emerging: Opinion stated with little supporting argument.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 affects the use of software.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The Act means software is automatically protected as intellectual property when created (1); copying or distributing software without permission from the rights holder is illegal (1); this applies even for personal use without commercial intent (1); organisations that use unlicensed software can face legal action or fines (1). Secure: Two points about software copyright explained clearly. Developing: Copying without permission is illegal — one point. Emerging: Mentions the Act with no specific software application.

glossary_terms.definition: Issues concerning what is morally right and wrong in the development and use of technology, where reasonable people may disagree.
Issues governed by laws that set clear boundaries on what is and is not permitted when using or developing technology.
Gaining access to a computer system or data without the permission of the owner — also called unauthorised access.
UK law passed in 2018 that regulates how organisations collect, store, process and share personal data, incorporating UK GDPR and giving individuals rights over their own data.

UK law passed in 1990 (with later amendments) that makes unauthorised access to computer systems, unauthorised access with intent to commit further offences, and unauthorised modification of computer material all criminal offences.
UK law passed in 1988 that protects creative works — including software, music, images, literature and film — from being copied, distributed or used without permission from the rights holder.

lessons.title: Autonomous Vehicles and Environmental Impacts
lessons.description: Self-driving car ethics, data centre energy use, e-waste and balancing digital benefit against harm.
lessons.content_html:
Autonomous Vehicles

An autonomous vehicle is a vehicle that can drive itself, using sensors (cameras, radar, lidar), artificial intelligence and real-time mapping to navigate roads without a human at the controls. Partially autonomous features — such as lane-keeping assistance, automatic braking and motorway cruise control — are already widely available. Fully self-driving taxis and freight lorries are being tested in several countries. The potential benefits are significant: reduced road accidents caused by human error, improved mobility for people who cannot drive, smoother traffic flow, and reduced need for parking in cities.

Ethical Challenges of Self-Driving Cars

Autonomous vehicles raise ethical questions that have no easy answers. These questions are sometimes framed around thought experiments involving unavoidable collision scenarios: if an autonomous vehicle cannot stop in time, should its algorithm prioritise the passenger, a pedestrian, or act in a way that minimises total harm? No consensus has emerged on how these algorithms should be programmed, and different cultural attitudes produce different intuitions.

Decision-making algorithms: When a collision is unavoidable, who or what should the vehicle’s programming prioritise? Choosing the passenger’s safety above others seems self-serving; choosing to minimise total harm treats the passenger as expendable. These decisions are currently made by engineers and, ultimately, by manufacturers — raising questions of accountability and transparency.

Liability after collisions: With a human driver, blame is relatively straightforward to assign. With an autonomous vehicle, responsibility may lie with the vehicle manufacturer, the software developer, the road authority, the person who set the destination, or some combination of all of these. Current legal frameworks are not well-equipped to deal with this complexity.

Displacement of workers: Large-scale adoption of autonomous vehicles would affect millions of people employed as taxi drivers, lorry drivers, bus drivers and delivery workers. The technology could improve safety and efficiency, but at a significant social cost to those workers and the communities that depend on those jobs. Retraining and social support would be needed at scale.

Security and hacking: An autonomous vehicle is essentially a computer on wheels. If its systems were hacked, a vehicle could be manipulated remotely — creating a physical safety risk as well as a digital security risk.

Key Fact

Three core ethical issues with autonomous vehicles: decision-making algorithms (who is prioritised in unavoidable accidents?), liability (who is legally responsible when an autonomous vehicle is involved in a collision?), and job displacement (what happens to millions of professional drivers?).

Environmental Impacts of Digital Technology

Digital technology is often described as “clean” compared with heavy industry, but its environmental footprint is substantial. There are three main categories of environmental impact: manufacturing, energy consumption in use, and disposal.

Manufacturing Impact

Producing electronic devices requires mining rare earth minerals and metals including lithium, cobalt, gold and tantalum. Mining operations can cause habitat destruction, water pollution and generate significant carbon emissions. The energy-intensive processes used to fabricate processors and circuit boards also contribute to carbon output. Every new device bought represents environmental cost before it has even been switched on.

Energy Consumption

Data centres power the internet, cloud storage, streaming services and online applications. Running servers continuously requires enormous amounts of electricity; cooling systems — which prevent equipment from overheating — consume additional power and water. As more services move online and global data traffic grows, the energy demands of data centres grow with it.

Individual devices also consume energy throughout their lifetimes. Keeping smartphones, laptops and televisions running adds up across billions of users. Wireless networks (mobile masts, Wi-Fi routers) require continuous power to operate.

Technology can also reduce environmental harm. Remote working and video conferencing reduce the need for commuting and business travel, cutting transport emissions. Digital documents replace paper, reducing deforestation. Smart energy-management systems in buildings use sensors and software to optimise heating and lighting, saving energy. Precision agriculture uses sensors and data analysis to apply fertilisers and water only where needed, reducing runoff. Monitoring systems can track wildlife, deforestation and pollution in real time, enabling faster responses to environmental damage.

E-Waste

E-waste (electronic waste) is one of the fastest-growing waste categories globally. Devices contain hazardous materials including lead, mercury and cadmium. When old devices end up in landfill, these substances can leach into soil and groundwater. In some parts of the world, informal recycling of e-waste exposes workers to toxic chemicals. Planned obsolescence — where manufacturers design products to have a limited lifespan or stop providing software updates after a few years — accelerates the rate at which devices are discarded.

Key Fact

E-waste is discarded electronic equipment containing hazardous materials. Planned obsolescence — designing products to become outdated quickly — increases e-waste by encouraging frequent replacement. Reducing e-waste requires longer device lifespans, easier repairability and responsible recycling schemes.

Reducing Environmental Impact

Several approaches can reduce the environmental impact of technology. Consumers can extend device lifespans by repairing rather than replacing, choosing refurbished devices, and using official recycling and take-back schemes rather than sending old electronics to general waste. Manufacturers can design products that are easier to repair, use more recycled materials, and provide software support for longer periods. Organisations can host their services on data centres that run on renewable energy or use waste heat recovery systems. Collectively, these choices reduce mining demand, energy consumption and toxic landfill.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For extended response questions on ethical or environmental topics, structure your answer around distinct points rather than writing a general essay. Each point should identify the issue, explain the mechanism (how it causes harm or benefit), and give a concrete example or consequence. For autonomous vehicles, common exam prompts ask you to discuss the “ethical implications” — make sure you cover both the benefits (safety, accessibility) and the harms (liability, job loss, algorithmic decision-making). For environmental topics, distinguish clearly between the three stages: manufacture, use and disposal.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Autonomous vehicles raise ethical issues around algorithmic decision-making in unavoidable accidents, liability after collisions, and large-scale displacement of professional drivers. Benefits include reduced human-error accidents and greater mobility.
  • Environmental impacts span the full device lifecycle: resource-intensive manufacturing, high energy consumption in data centres and during use, and toxic e-waste at disposal. Planned obsolescence worsens e-waste by shortening device lifespans.
  • Technology can also reduce environmental harm through remote working, smart energy systems, precision agriculture and environmental monitoring — exam answers should present both sides in a balanced way.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ethical issues raised by autonomous vehicles.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Decision-making algorithms — in an unavoidable collision, the programming must choose who to prioritise, which raises questions about whose life matters more and how that decision is made (1+1). Liability — when an autonomous vehicle causes a collision, it is unclear whether responsibility lies with the manufacturer, software developer or owner, because current legal frameworks assume a human driver (1+1). Secure: Two issues described with explanation. Developing: Two issues named without adequate explanation. Emerging: One issue named.

practice_questions.text: Explain what e-waste is and describe one environmental risk it causes.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: E-waste is discarded electronic devices and components such as old phones, laptops and circuit boards (1); these devices contain hazardous materials such as lead, mercury or cadmium (1); when sent to landfill these toxic substances leach into soil and groundwater (1); this can contaminate drinking water sources and harm ecosystems (1). Secure: Definition correct and one risk clearly explained. Developing: Definition partially correct or risk vague. Emerging: E-waste mentioned with no explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why data centres have a significant environmental impact.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Data centres house hundreds or thousands of servers running continuously (1); this requires large amounts of electricity to power the servers (1); cooling systems are also needed to prevent overheating, consuming additional electricity and water (1); as online services and cloud storage grow, data centre energy demands increase further (1). Secure: Two aspects (power + cooling) explained. Developing: Energy use mentioned without cooling or growth angle. Emerging: Data centres use electricity — no further development.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by planned obsolescence and describe one environmental consequence.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Planned obsolescence is the practice of designing products to become outdated or stop receiving software updates after a limited period (1); this encourages consumers to replace devices sooner than would otherwise be necessary (1); this increases the volume of e-waste generated (1); more devices are discarded, adding toxic materials to landfill and increasing demand for mining of new raw materials (1). Secure: Definition and one environmental consequence clearly linked. Developing: Planned obsolescence described but consequence vague. Emerging: Term used but not explained.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that autonomous vehicles will have a more positive than negative impact on society.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Positive — reduces road accidents caused by human error (fatigue, distraction, impairment) (developed point); improves mobility for elderly, disabled or those unable to drive (developed point); smoother traffic flow reduces fuel waste; allows passengers to use travel time productively. Negative — displaces taxi, lorry, bus and delivery drivers at scale with social consequences; algorithmic decision-making in collisions is ethically unresolved; liability after accidents is legally complex; vehicles are vulnerable to hacking. Conclusion — weighs both sides and reaches a justified judgement. Secure: Both sides addressed with some development and a conclusion. Developing: One side well-developed, other side listed. Emerging: Opinion stated with minimal supporting argument.

practice_questions.text: State two ways that individuals can help reduce the environmental impact of their electronic devices.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Repair or buy refurbished devices rather than buying new (1); use official recycling or take-back schemes rather than sending old devices to general landfill (1). Secure: Any two distinct methods. Developing: One correct method. Emerging: General comment about caring for the environment.
